entries.proposition: The review is sponsor-authored: authors are employees and stockholders of the drug developer, and writing support was funded by it.
entries.snippet: S.K. and K.N. are employees of, and stockholders in, Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Limited.

entries.proposition: The mechanism of soticlestat is stated as undetermined; the review presents a working hypothesis from preclinical data.
entries.snippet: The exact mechanisms of action by which soticlestat exerts pharmacological benefits, such as reducing seizure frequency as seen in the ELEKTRA phase II study in patients with Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, 3 remains to be fully elucidated.

entries.proposition: Total brain cholesterol stays unchanged when CH24H is deleted in mice, because de novo synthesis falls; this is a homeostasis premise relevant to measuring cholesterol alone.
entries.snippet: For example, when CH24H was deleted in mice, total brain cholesterol remained unchanged.

entries.proposition: More than 95 percent of brain cholesterol is synthesised within the brain and the barrier prevents exchange with blood, so peripheral lipid levels do not set brain supply.
entries.snippet: Consequently, >95% of brain cholesterol is synthesized de novo within astrocytes.

entries.proposition: Mouse efficacy is model-dependent: soticlestat protected in the Dravet models, kainate model, kindling and audiogenic models but not in maximal electroshock, subcutaneous pentylenetetrazol or 6-Hz assays.
entries.snippet: Soticlestat was ineffective in the maximal electroshock model of generalized tonic–clonic seizures, a “gold standard” in epilepsy drug screening

entries.proposition: Table 2 gives eight protected-per-tested counts per arm in the screening models.
entries.snippet: Maximum electroshock seizures model | Mouse a | Vehicle | 0/8

entries.proposition: Mechanism 1 rests on 24-hydroxycholesterol as a positive allosteric modulator of NMDA receptors; knockout slices show a smaller NMDA/AMPA ratio without change in intrinsic excitability, spontaneous transmission or long-term potentiation.
entries.snippet: Slices from CH24H knockout mice showed a significantly smaller NMDAR to α‐amino‐3‐hydroxy‐5‐methyl‐4‐isoxazoleproprionic acid receptor

entries.proposition: The authors say the strong correlation between brain drug level and 24-hydroxycholesterol is why the effect is likely mediated by the metabolite; this is stated as likely, not shown.
entries.snippet: Therefore, it is likely that the antiseizure effect of soticlestat is primarily exerted through reduction of brain 24HC.

entries.proposition: Mechanism 2 (membrane raft cholesterol and glutamate transporter EAAT2) is a hypothesis drawn from astrocyte overexpression work.
entries.snippet: Inhibition of CH24H by soticlestat is hypothesized to preserve the membrane raft structure by inhibiting conversion of membrane cholesterol in the raft.

entries.proposition: Mechanism 3 (neuroinflammation) rests on a correlation between brain 24-hydroxycholesterol and TNF-alpha in a tauopathy mouse model, which the authors say may be consequence of tissue damage rather than cause.
entries.snippet: Because of the vicious cycle of neuroinflammation in epilepsy, it was unclear whether the correlation between 24HC and TNF‐α was a direct causal relationship or a consequence of tissue damage.

entries.proposition: The review closes by stating the second and third mechanisms need further study; no clinical efficacy figures are reported in it.
entries.snippet: These potential mechanisms of action, especially the second and third, warrant future studies to gain further insights into the antiseizure effects of soticlestat.

entries.proposition: PANEL READING, the summary scheme (matches the Figure 3 legend): numbered branches 1 to 3 from cholesterol and CH24H to 24-hydroxycholesterol, TNF-alpha, membrane raft cholesterol, glutamate in the cleft, NMDA/AMPA receptors and hyperexcitation; red arrows for the pathogenic state and green for soticlestat effects. A schematic, no data.
